impact_evidence: [design] guess; [corrected by fact-check: Frechette, Lizzeri & Salz 2019 model NYC taxi search frictions and find increasing returns to scale in matching; they do not estimate rider multi-homing or platform competition]; cross-link R06
applies_to: human app driver, taxi, robotaxi, fleet
how_to_model: Rider samples k options and picks lowest generalised cost (price + value of time x ETA)

name: Ride product choice
description: Which product the rider books (UberX, Comfort, XL, Black, WAV, Share, Pet, Car Seat; Lyft tiers), which decides which vehicles may take the trip.
values_or_range: Standard tier dominant (~80%+ [U]); XL/Black pay more per trip
impact_evidence: [P*] HVFHV Parquet columns confirmed: only shared and WAV flags, no product field, so the product split is not public
data_source: none found for product split (only shared_request_flag, wav_request_flag)
how_to_model: Multinomial logit over products using price ratio and party size; vehicle eligibility from R08

name: Mode alternatives (subway, bus, Citi Bike, walking, own car)
description: How good the other ways to make the same trip are, which shapes how many people choose a car.
values_or_range: Citi Bike faster than taxi for ~40% of taxi trips (2017) [uncertain: share not re-read; Schneider's comparison used Jul 2016-Jun 2017 trips between Citi Bike stations]; late-night subway headways ~20 min [U]
impact_evidence: [S] Todd Schneider 2017 taxi vs Citi Bike; [S] Hall et al. 2018 transit complement
data_source: MTA GTFS and ridership (data.ny.gov); Citi Bike system data https://citibikenyc.com/system-data
how_to_model: Nested logit or zone-hour multiplier from transit level of service

name: Transit disruption substitution
description: Extra car demand near stations when a subway line is delayed or closed.
values_or_range: Each subway disruption displaces >1,500 rides but adds <40 taxi, ride-hail and Citi Bike rides; station closures +2.8-3.3% ride-share use
impact_evidence: [S] NYU Stern ridesharing and public transport study [uncertain: figures not re-read]; cross-link R03
how_to_model: On disruption, add ~2-5% of displaced riders as requests in affected station zones

name: Household car access by home zone
description: Share of households without a car, which raises baseline taxi and app demand where car ownership is low.
values_or_range: Manhattan ~20-25% of households own a car vs ~45% citywide [U]
impact_evidence: [U] ACS vehicles available; already embedded in TLC baseline, matters for synthetic or non-NYC cities
data_source: US Census ACS table B25044 https://data.census.gov
how_to_model: Covariate in a gravity/generation model when generalising beyond NYC

name: Transit alternatives to the airports
description: The price and reliability of rail and bus links to JFK, LGA and EWR, which cap how many travellers take a car and how sharply that share falls when surge is high. Generalises to any city with airport rail or bus links.
values_or_range: AirTrain JFK costs $8.50, plus subway or LIRR. It was half price ($4.25) from 30 Jun to Labor Day (1 Sep) 2025 at Jamaica and Howard Beach, as also in summer 2024. AirTrain JFK carried about 11.7M riders in 2025 (6.7M in 2023), about 30.7k per weekday in Q1 2026. The Q70 LaGuardia Link has been fare-free since 1 May 2022; its 2024 ridership was about 25% above 2019. EWR: AirTrain Newark plus NJ Transit or Amtrak. Outages are in R03-049.
impact_evidence: [S] NY1, Frommers and 6sqft (Jun 2025) on the half-price AirTrain. [S] The Points Guy (1 May 2022) and an MTA service document on the fare-free Q70. [S] AirTrain ridership via Wikipedia only; the PANYNJ figure was not read.
data_source: PANYNJ airport traffic reports https://www.panynj.gov/airports/en/statistics-general-info.html ; MTA ridership (data.ny.gov); MTA airport guides https://www.mta.info/guides/airports/laguardia
how_to_model: Airport-trip mode choice (nested logit on fare, time, luggage and hour). Transit fares are rule inputs, with scenario toggles for fare changes or outages.

name: Pre-match abandonment and 'no cars available'
description: How long a rider keeps waiting while the app is still searching for a car, and the platform rule that refuses or hides service when no car is within an ETA threshold. This is pre-match; post-match cancels are R05-022.
values_or_range: Search patience: median 1-3 min, then the rider abandons or switches app or mode [design]. 'No cars available' when the best ETA exceeds 15-25 min [design]. Abandonment 0-10% of requests citywide, far higher at night in outer zones [design].
impact_evidence: [design]. [P, from list] Castillo, Knoepfle & Weyl: in thin hours and areas, riders cancel and waits jump (R06-039). TLC records hold completed trips only, so no public abandonment rate exists.
applies_to: human app driver; robotaxi; fleet; taxi e-hail
data_source: none found (unmatched requests are not published)
how_to_model: Each unmatched request draws a patience time. It leaves (to a rival, to a taxi hail, or lost) when patience runs out or the platform ETA threshold is exceeded. Feeds R06-022 and R06-039.

name: Riders moving out of surge zones
description: When surge or ETA is high, some riders walk to a cheaper or better-served neighbouring zone, or move the pickup pin, so demand leaks across surge boundaries.
values_or_range: 0-15% of surge-exposed requests move 100-400 m [design]; no NYC estimate found.
impact_evidence: [design]; [U] rider walking is widely reported, but no NYC estimate was found.
how_to_model: For requests facing surge above a threshold, move the origin with probability p to an adjacent zone with lower surge or ETA, and add walk time.

name: Rider promotions and memberships on incumbent apps
description: Promo codes, Uber One and Lyft Pink memberships and corporate vouchers lower a rider's price on one app without changing driver pay, which shifts demand between apps.
values_or_range: Uber One gives 6% back in Uber Cash on rides (it replaced a 5% discount in 2023); Lyft Pink gives about 5% off rides; both cost $9.99/month [S]. Uber One reportedly had about 50M members accounting for over half of Uber gross bookings in Q1 2026 [S, secondary summary]. Short promotions of 5-20% off on one app for 1-7 days [design].
impact_evidence: [S] TechCrunch (May 2023) on Uber One's switch to cash back; RideWise and Ridesharing Driver comparisons (2025-26); Briefing.com Q1 2026 summary. It matters for a multi-apping driver (R06-034) because it moves request share between apps while pay stays the same.
applies_to: human app driver (multi-app), fleet on a platform
how_to_model: A time-limited multiplier on each app's demand share (R05-004) and on riders' price elasticity, with driver pay unchanged. Members get a standing 5-6% price cut on their home app.

name: Riders who defer during surge and request again
description: Some riders who balk at a surge price postpone the trip rather than drop it and check again 5-30 minutes later, so demand returns as the price falls.
values_or_range: Of riders who balk at a surge quote, 20-60% defer, and 40-80% of those request again within 5-30 min [design guess]. Lyft's CEO said Wait & Save (cheaper in exchange for a longer wait) was about 30% of Lyft rides in Q1 2023 [S]. Lyft said NYC averaged more than 150,000 Wait & Save rides a week in Q2 2023 [S], roughly 13% of Lyft's ~1.1M weekly NYC trips (4.90M Lyft trips in Jan 2023 HVFHV data) [design calc; added by fact-check]. So many riders trade time for price.
impact_evidence: [S] FOX Business interview with Lyft CEO Risher (no primary filing found) and Lyft Q2 2023 earnings call. Deferral flattens and lengthens peaks, so arriving 'late' to a fading surge can still pay; R05-020 treats every lost request as gone [design].
applies_to: human app driver, robotaxi, fleet (own pricing, G2-026)
data_source: none found (TLC records hold completed trips only)
how_to_model: Balked requests go into a deferral pool and come back over 5-30 min, re-quoted at the price at that time. Calibrate together with R05-020 and R05-066.

name: Party size
description: Number of riders per request, which decides XL eligibility and shared-ride feasibility.
values_or_range: [corrected by fact-check: yellow 2023 passenger_count is 1 rider 75.2%, 2 riders 15.2%, 3 riders 3.8%, 4 riders 2.1%, 5-6 riders 2.2%, 0 (entry error) 1.6%; was '1 ~70%, 3-4 ~10%, 5+ ~2% [U]']; yellow counts are driver-entered; HVFHV files have no passenger count
impact_evidence: [P*] own calc on local TLC Parquet copies (yellow 2023, 37M trips; same result in R08 data folder); [S] CMU capstone
data_source: TLC yellow and green passenger_count (none in HVFHV)
how_to_model: Sample from empirical distribution by hour and purpose (nightlife groups larger)

name: Luggage and trunk need
description: Bags that need trunk space, mostly on airport and hotel trips, adding loading time and vehicle needs.
values_or_range: Airport trips 1-3 bags; +1-2 min loading [design guess]
impact_evidence: [design]; robotaxi has no driver to help load
how_to_model: Bag count by purpose; capacity check vs vehicle (R08); adds boarding time

name: Wheelchair-accessible (WAV) requests
description: Requests that need a wheelchair-accessible vehicle, with service-time standards set by TLC.
values_or_range: [corrected by fact-check: the '90% within 10 min' standard is in force, not just proposed: 35 RCNY 59B-17(f)(3)(i), amended eff. 6 Mar 2025, requires approved Accessible Vehicle dispatchers (the route Uber and Lyft use [U]) to serve 90% of WAV requests in under 10 min; the alternative is sending 25% of all trips to WAVs (59B-17(c)(1)); the earlier 80%/10 min and 90%/15 min standard was not re-checked]; WAV fleet >7,600 (Oct 2024) [S]; 88% picked up within 10 min (2024) [S]; WAV requests are 0.15% of HVFHV trips and 6.6% of trips are served by a WAV (Jan 2023)
impact_evidence: [P*] 35 RCNY 59B-17 (verbatim RCNY copy, github.com/jehiah/nyc_code_archive); [S] TLC FHV annual accessibility report 2024; [P*] own calc on local TLC Parquet copies (wav_request_flag, wav_match_flag)
applies_to: human app driver, taxi, fleet, robotaxi
data_source: TLC HVFHV wav_request_flag/wav_match_flag; TLC accessibility reports
how_to_model: WAV requests only matchable to WAV vehicles; boarding +5-10 min; fleet must meet service standard (R07)

name: Shared-ride requests and match rate
description: Requests for a shared ride and how often they actually get paired with another rider.
values_or_range: UberX Share relaunched in NYC June 2022 [uncertain: date not re-checked]; up to 20% off; designed to add ~8 min on average [S]; [fact-check: Jan 2023 shared requests were 2.6% of HVFHV trips (Uber 1.7%, Lyft 5.4%) and matched shared trips 1.0% (Uber 0.3%, Lyft 2.8%), so the '<5%' guess holds]
impact_evidence: [S] Uber newsroom 'Introducing UberX Share'; [P*] own calc on local TLC Parquet copies (shared_request_flag, shared_match_flag)
how_to_model: Share option in product choice; pooling handled in matching (R06)

name: Multi-stop trips
description: Trips with extra stops on the way, each adding waiting time.
values_or_range: Up to 3 stops [U]; 2-8% of trips; +1-5 min per stop [design guess]
impact_evidence: [design]
how_to_model: Bernoulli extra stop with dwell time; fare adds time component

name: Scheduled and reserved rides
description: Rides booked ahead (for example early airport trips), known to the system before they start.
values_or_range: 1-3% of trips [design guess]; booking lead from hours to weeks
impact_evidence: [design]; gives the agent advance demand information
how_to_model: Pre-announced requests released to the agent with lead time; can be accepted ahead

name: Child car seat and pet requests
description: Requests that need a car seat or allow a pet, which only some vehicles serve, sometimes at a surcharge.
values_or_range: Uber Car Seat in NYC: $10 surcharge, one seat per ride; pet requests <1% [U]
impact_evidence: [S] TechCrunch 2014 uberFAMILY; The Points Guy 2024
how_to_model: Rare request flags requiring equipped vehicle; surcharge added

name: Service animals and other riders who must be carried
description: Riders with service animals or folded mobility devices must be carried; refusing them counts as a service refusal, with fines and possible loss of the licence or app account. The ADA gives a similar duty across the US.
values_or_range: 0.1-0.5% of requests come with a service animal [design guess]. Refusing one is a service refusal. For taxis the penalty is $350 / $500 (pleaded / after hearing) for a first offence, rising to $750 / $1,000 plus licence revocation for a third within 36 months (35 RCNY 80-20, R07-042). App deactivation risk [U]. The animal is not revealed until pickup.
impact_evidence: [S] TLC Industry Notice 10-28 (29 Nov 2010, repeating 09-23): service animals must be admitted in all taxis and FHVs, secured or not; refusal is a service refusal, with penalties up to licence suspension or revocation. A Dec 2020 TLC amendment updated the service-animal wording [S]. [P*, from list] penalty table in R07-042. [U] ADA 49 CFR 37.167(d). [corrected: dated '$300-1,000' fines replaced by the current penalty table].
applies_to: all (a robotaxi must carry them too)
how_to_model: Request flag revealed at pickup. Refusal triggers a fine or deactivation draw (R07-042) and a compliance-panel entry (R12-059).

name: Mid-trip destination changes and repricing
description: Riders change or mistype the destination or add stops after pickup, and the platform reprices the fare and driver pay on actual time and distance. Stops entered before the trip are R05-033.
values_or_range: 1-3% of app trips [design guess]. NYC-specific address traps include hyphenated Queens addresses and street names repeated across boroughs [U]. The 120% cap on the fare estimate does not apply when the passenger alters the route, including the destination, number of stops, vehicle type or a toll route (35 RCNY 59B-23, via R07-022) [P*, re-read by fact-check]. Taxi trips are metered, so they need no repricing.
impact_evidence: [P*] 35 RCNY 59B-23 rule text; [U] Uber/Lyft help pages on fare adjustment. This weakens decisions based on the upfront offer (R06-025).
applies_to: human app driver, robotaxi (rider edits in the app), fleet
data_source: none found (TLC data records only the final drop-off)
how_to_model: With a small probability per trip, redraw the destination mid-trip or add a stop. Recompute fare and pay on actual miles and minutes, and log the quote-vs-final gap.

name: Rider no-show
description: Rider never appears at the pickup, so the driver waits and then cancels for a fee.
values_or_range: 1-5% of matched trips [design guess]; wait 5 min before no-show fee (2016 NYC pilot); fee $5-$10+ [uncertain: 2026 NYC wait and fee amounts not confirmed; see R07-035]
impact_evidence: [S] TechCrunch Apr 2016 on Uber wait/no-show pilot in NYC
applies_to: human app driver, robotaxi, taxi e-hail
how_to_model: Bernoulli no-show with night and nightlife uplift; agent chooses when to cancel; fee per R07

name: Rider lateness at pickup
description: Time between the car arriving and the rider getting in.
values_or_range: [corrected by fact-check: for Uber completed trips in Jan 2023, on-scene to pickup is median 0.8 min, mean 1.0 min, p90 2.0 min; 12.8% wait over 2 min and 0.5% over 5 min; was 'median 1-2 min [design guess]']; wait-time fee after 2 min [S]
impact_evidence: [S] TechCrunch 2016 (2-min wait fee); [P*] own calc on local TLC Parquet copies (on_scene_datetime vs pickup_datetime; completed trips only, so no-shows are excluded)
applies_to: human app driver, robotaxi, taxi e-hail
data_source: TLC HVFHV on_scene_datetime [corrected by fact-check: the dictionary says 'Accessible Vehicles-only', but in Jan 2023 Uber (HV0003) fills it on 100% of trips and Lyft (HV0005) on ~0.1%]
how_to_model: Lognormal delay by segment (elderly, luggage, groups slower)

name: Designated pickup areas
description: Places where app riders must walk to a set pickup zone, such as airports, stadiums and some venues.
values_or_range: Rider walk 3-15 min; dedicated lots at JFK and LGA [S]
impact_evidence: [S] Uber JFK driver information page (cell phone lot, virtual queue)
data_source: Uber airport pages; Port Authority ground transport pages
how_to_model: Map pickups at these POIs to fixed pickup nodes with rider walk delay (cross-link R01, R03)

name: Street hail vs e-hail channel share
description: Split of taxi demand between people hailing on the street and people booking a taxi through an app.
values_or_range: Yellow e-hail share ~5-15% [U]; ~14,000 cabs in 2022 Uber-Curb-Arro beta [S]; green trip_type separates hail from dispatch [fact-check: green Oct 2019 is 79.4% street hail (1), 1.9% dispatch (2), 18.8% blank]
impact_evidence: [S] Al Jazeera 2022 on Uber listing NYC cabs; [P*] own calc on local TLC Parquet copies (green trip_type, Oct 2019)
data_source: TLC green trip_type; yellow has no channel flag
how_to_model: Split taxi demand into hail stream and dispatched stream

name: Street-hail encounters and hail rights
description: Chance an empty taxi meets a hailing rider, given foot traffic and how many empty taxis pass first; plus who may street-hail where.
values_or_range: Yellow anywhere (only yellow in the Manhattan core and at airports); green only outside that zone; app cars and robotaxis never; 0-2 hails per block-minute [design].
impact_evidence: Medallions grant street-hail rights citywide [S]; green Hail Exclusionary Zone = Manhattan south of E 96th St and W 110th St plus the NYC airports [verified by fact-check: was 'zone rules [U]'; P*, 35 RCNY 51-03].
data_source: Yellow and green pickups by zone (TLC); foot traffic (R01)
how_to_model: Hail arrivals per street segment; the first empty eligible taxi to pass gets it.

name: Street hailers' direction bias (taxi)
description: Street hailers mostly flag cabs already heading their way, so the avenue and direction a cab cruises on shapes where its riders want to go.
values_or_range: On one-way avenues, 60-85% of hailers have a destination ahead of the cab [design guess]. The effect is weaker on two-way streets and at taxi stands.
impact_evidence: [U] taxi-driver lore. TLC data is zone-level with no heading, so it can only partly test this. It matters most for steering toward home or the garage at shift end (R05-060) [design].
applies_to: taxi (street hail); not app cars or robotaxis
data_source: none found (TLC yellow records give pickup and drop-off zones only)
how_to_model: Condition each hail's destination on the cab's heading by tilting the R05-006 destination weights toward zones ahead of it on its one-way street.

name: Wrong-rider pickups at crowded curbs
description: At crowded let-outs and hubs a driver can pick up the wrong rider, or spend extra minutes finding the right one, unless PIN verification is used.
values_or_range: 0.1-1% of pickups at crowded curbs, costing 2-10 min and sometimes an unpaid wrong trip [design]. Uber's optional PIN verification was shown in Sep 2019, piloted in 7 cities and rolled out to all US and Canada riders in Jan 2020; when it is on, a trip cannot start until the driver enters the PIN [S; corrected by fact-check, was 'since 2019 [U]']. Robotaxi: the rider unlocks the car in the app, so wrong-rider risk is near zero, but finding the car can take longer [design].
impact_evidence: [design]; [S] Inverse and local news (Jan 2020) on the PIN rollout. R10-039 and R05-040 cover pin error and R10-040 covers curb queues, but none covers wrong-rider events.
applies_to: human app driver; robotaxi (finding the car)
how_to_model: A mismatch probability that rises with the number of cars and riders at the pickup node (R10-040), set to zero for riders with PIN on. Each event adds delay, or an unpaid trip plus a rider cancellation.

name: Ratings riders give the driver
description: Star ratings riders leave, driven by wait, route, cleanliness and conduct, feeding the driver's rating.
values_or_range: Mostly 5 stars; 1-3 low ratings per 100 trips rising with delays [design guess]
impact_evidence: [design]; matters through deactivation risk in R09
how_to_model: P(rating | service quality) updates driver rating state (R09)

name: Rider rating shown to driver
description: The rider's own rating shown on the offer, a weak signal of no-show, mess or low tips.
values_or_range: Average rider ~4.89 (third party); NYC riders get the lowest ratings [uncertain: not re-checked]; low-rated riders can lose access (Uber, 2019)
impact_evidence: [S] Uber 2019 announcement (USA Today); [S] third-party FAQs
how_to_model: Request attribute correlated with no-show, incident and tip propensity

name: Rider safety incidents
description: Rare assaults, robberies or harassment involving riders or drivers.
values_or_range: 99.9% of Uber US trips had no reported safety incident (2017-18); 20 physical-assault deaths in 2019-20 (15 riders) [uncertain: rider/driver split not re-checked]
impact_evidence: [S] Uber US Safety Reports (press coverage)
how_to_model: Rare event with night and zone multipliers; trip lost, downtime, may end shift (R09)

name: Vomit, mess and cleaning fee
description: A rider makes a mess, the car goes off duty for cleaning and the rider is charged a fee.
values_or_range: Uber tiers $20 small, $40 vomit, $80 large spill, $150 heavy bodily fluids; 1 per 500-2,000 late-weekend trips [design guess]
impact_evidence: [S] Uber fee tiers via local news on 'vomit fraud'
how_to_model: P(mess | nightlife, hour) leads to 30-90 min downtime plus fee and dispute chance

name: Lost items and return fees
description: Items riders leave behind, which the driver can return for a fee.
values_or_range: $20 return fee to driver (Uber Canada 2023; older $15); 0.5-1% of trips [design guess]
impact_evidence: [S] Uber Canada 2023 Lost and Found Index; Tile 2024 analysis
how_to_model: Bernoulli lost item; agent decides return detour vs keep driving

name: Fare disputes, refunds and chargebacks
description: Riders who complain about route or fees and get money back, sometimes clawed from the driver.
values_or_range: 0.5-2% of trips disputed [design guess]; complaints of false cleaning fees rising
impact_evidence: [S] BBB-cited 'vomit fraud' complaints in press
how_to_model: Dispute chance rises with detour vs shortest path and ETA slip; payout rule from R07

name: Non-payment and fare evasion
description: Taxi riders who run off without paying or whose card fails.
values_or_range: 0.1-0.5% of cash taxi trips [design guess]
impact_evidence: [design]
how_to_model: Bernoulli loss of fare on cash trips, higher late night

sub_box: Destination value, stranding and airport demand
name: Destination re-dispatch value
description: Expected wait for the next paying trip after dropping off in a zone, which makes some fares worth more than their price.
values_or_range: Manhattan core 1-5 min vs outer Queens or Staten Island 10-30+ min [design guess]
impact_evidence: [design] computable from TLC pickups and drop-offs; central to accept/decline and positioning
how_to_model: Emerges from demand plus supply; harness logs idle time after each drop

sub_box: Destination value, stranding and airport demand
name: Out-of-city trips and stranding
description: Trips to Nassau, Westchester, New Jersey or Newark that pay well but leave the car far from demand.
values_or_range: Taxis must serve NYC, Nassau, Westchester and Newark Airport [fact-check: confirmed, 35 RCNY 80-20(a)(1); a driver who has operated more than 8 h may refuse EWR, Nassau and Westchester, 80-20(b)(8)]; [corrected by fact-check: 4.5% of HVFHV trips end outside the city (3.9% in zone 265 + 0.6% at EWR; avg 16.6 mi, avg driver pay $44.6, Jan 2023) and 0.7% of yellow trips (2023), not '1-3% [U]'; HVFHV pickups in zone 265 are ~0.005% of trips, so the return is almost always empty]; empty return 30-90 min [design guess]
impact_evidence: [P*] 35 RCNY 80-20 (verbatim RCNY copy); [P*] taxi zone lookup: 1 = Newark Airport, 265 = Outside of NYC; [P*] own calc on local TLC Parquet copies (also R08 data folder)
data_source: TLC DOLocationID (1 = EWR, 265 = Outside of NYC; confirmed in zone lookup); yellow RatecodeID 3 Newark, 4 Nassau/Westchester, 5 negotiated
how_to_model: External destination nodes; low return-match chance; tolls on return (R07)

sub_box: Destination value, stranding and airport demand
name: Airport-bound demand (departures)
description: Requests to JFK, LGA and EWR, tied to flight departure times.
values_or_range: Early-morning wave: airport-bound share of weekday HVFHV trips peaks at 24-28% at 04:00-06:00; volume peaks at 05:00 with a second bump at 13:00-16:00 [fact-check: own calc, Jan 2023]; JFK yellow flat fare $70 (Dec 2022 rule) [fact-check: confirmed in 2023 yellow records, RatecodeID 2 fare $70]
impact_evidence: [S] TLC 2022 fare rule coverage: JFK flat fare $52 to $70; [P*] own calc on local TLC Parquet copies; [P*] 35 RCNY 58-26 (via R07)
data_source: BTS on-time and schedule data https://www.transtats.bts.gov/; TLC DOLocationID 132 JFK, 138 LGA, 1 EWR (confirmed in zone lookup)
how_to_model: Departures by hour minus 2-3 h lead, x origin shares from TLC

sub_box: Destination value, stranding and airport demand
name: Airport arrival demand
description: Requests from arriving passengers, driven by flight arrival waves and how many choose a taxi or app car.
values_or_range: LGA 42% by cab + 14% black car (2012-14); 41% of JFK and 63% of LGA travellers use taxi/limo/e-hail [uncertain: survey shares not re-read]; [fact-check: Jan 2023 airport pickups per day: JFK ~11,170 app vs ~5,160 yellow (app 68%), LGA ~9,920 app vs ~2,880 yellow (app 78%); airports are 8.6% of yellow pickups but 3.5% of HVFHV pickups, consistent with ride-hail taking airport share]
impact_evidence: [S] Port Authority survey via PANYNJ indicators; [S] 2021 airport access study; [P*] own calc on local TLC Parquet copies
data_source: BTS arrivals; PANYNJ traffic reports; 'Taxis Dispatched at Port Authority of NY NJ Airports' dataset (data.gov)
how_to_model: Arrivals x passengers per flight x mode share, released 20-60 min after landing at terminal pickup areas

sub_box: Destination value, stranding and airport demand
name: Airport passenger destination and fare mix
description: Where airport passengers go (Manhattan, Brooklyn, Long Island, NJ) and so what the trip pays.
values_or_range: JFK to Manhattan flat $70 (yellow, confirmed); LGA metered; [corrected by fact-check: Jan 2023 yellow plus HVFHV airport pickups go JFK -> Manhattan 39%, Queens 24%, Brooklyn 21%, outside NYC 14%; LGA -> Manhattan 57%, Brooklyn 15%, Queens 15%, outside NYC 9%; half of yellow JFK pickups use the flat fare (RatecodeID 2)]
impact_evidence: [P*] own calc on local TLC Parquet copies; [S] 2022 TLC rate rule coverage
data_source: TLC trips with PULocationID 132, 138, 1 (zone IDs confirmed)
how_to_model: Empirical destination distribution for airport pickups

sub_box: Destination value, stranding and airport demand
name: Flight delays shifting airport demand
description: Late or cancelled flights move or remove arrival waves.
values_or_range: Waves shift 15-180 min; storm days cancel banks [design guess]
impact_evidence: [design]; cross-link R03 and R04
how_to_model: Replay real arrival times per scenario day

sub_box: Destination value, stranding and airport demand
name: Landing-to-curb lag (deplaning, immigration, baggage)
description: The delay between a flight reaching the gate and its passengers requesting or hailing a ride, which is short for domestic flights and long and variable for international ones.
values_or_range: Domestic about 15-35 min after gate arrival [U]. International about 40-90+ min, of which the CBP passport queue is about 15-60+ min [S]. JFK: FlightQueue's estimate from historical CBP data is about 26 min for US citizens and 37-48 min for non-US citizens [S; corrected by fact-check: a third-party estimate, not an official CBP average]. Peaks run well over 1 h (a U.S. Travel Association report cited 4.5 h at JFK in Dec 2012) [S]. LGA is almost all domestic, JFK heavily international and EWR mixed [U]. This refines the flat 20-60 min release window in R05-062.
impact_evidence: [S] FlightQueue estimate (above). [S] Global Gateway Alliance analysis of CBP data, reported Dec 2013: kiosks at JFK Terminal 4 cut the average wait from 34.9 to 16.6 min and the maximum from 97 to 58 min within a month of installation (Oct to Nov 2013; the blog's '2012' baseline date looks like a typo). Joining the queue at the scheduled landing of an international bank is about an hour early [design].
applies_to: all (airport pickups); taxi via the holding lot; fleet airport allocation (R11-024)
data_source: CBP Airport Wait Times https://awt.cbp.gov (hourly average and maximum waits by airport and terminal; host not reachable from this session) [U]. BTS On-Time Performance https://www.transtats.bts.gov/ gives gate-in times for domestic nonstop flights of reporting US carriers ONLY, so it misses all international arrivals [S, corrected by fact-check]. For international arrival times: airport flight-status pages or OpenSky Network ADS-B landing data [U]. PANYNJ monthly airport traffic reports give the domestic/international passenger split [U].
how_to_model: For each arriving flight, release requests at gate time plus a lognormal lag set by domestic/international and terminal, with the CBP part drawn from that hour's published wait. This replaces the fixed 20-60 min offset in R05-062. Generalises to any airport through its international share.

name: Seasonal and holiday driver supply
description: How many drivers are working changes with season and holidays (vacations abroad, Ramadan, Christmas), changing competition.
values_or_range: Unknown magnitude; proxy: rider waits by month and holiday (NYD 01h median wait 8.6 vs 4.8 min)
impact_evidence: [P*] own calc, TLC HVFHV Jan 2023 (wait proxy); monthly active-driver counts not read [U]
applies_to: human app driver, taxi, robotaxi, fleet
data_source: NYC TLC HVFHV trip records, https://www.nyc.gov/site/tlc/about/tlc-trip-record-data.page; TLC monthly industry reports (driver counts)
how_to_model: Driver supply multiplier by month and holiday in R06, calibrated so waits match

name: Driver strikes and protests
description: Organised refusals to work or to serve a place, which cut competitor supply for a while.
values_or_range: e.g. LGA pickup strike 26 Feb 2023, noon to midnight; Uber claimed 36% more LGA trips that day; 0-3 a year.
impact_evidence: Gothamist and Fox Business reports [S].
how_to_model: Scenario event removing 10-60% of bots from a zone and window; announced in advance in event-aware runs.

name: Religious and cultural supply dips
description: Competitor supply drops around iftar in Ramadan and Friday midday prayers, since many NYC drivers are Muslim.
values_or_range: -5% to -25% supply for 30-60 min at sunset in Ramadan [design]; Friday 12-2 pm dip [U].
impact_evidence: Uber France reported an evening driver drop in Ramadan 2017 (Paris) [S]; NYC not measured.
data_source: None for NYC; test in HVFHV on-scene times
how_to_model: Calendar-driven break hazard for a share of bots.

name: Event let-out convergence
description: Competitors flock to stadium, concert and venue exits, so a known event draws extra supply and shortens surge.
values_or_range: 0.5-3x normal supply within 1 km in the 30 min before let-out [design].
impact_evidence: Supply rises with surge (Chen & Sheldon) [S]; size [design].
how_to_model: Share of bots that know the event schedule; tie to the with/without event-info treatment so rivals and agent are matched.

name: Competitor cars online by zone and hour
description: Number of other app cars and taxis logged on (busy or idle) in each taxi zone in each 15-minute slot.
values_or_range: NYC app cars online: about 15k on average (15-17k if utilisation is nearer 53%), about 25-30k at the evening peak, about 4-6k before dawn [design calc: ~667k trips/day x ~19 min / ~0.58 utilisation]; plus about 3-5k yellow taxis on the road in a daytime hour [corrected by fact-check: was 5-8k [U]; ~130k yellow trips/day x ~16 min / ~0.5-0.6 occupancy gives ~2.5-3k on average, x ~1.5 at peak [design calc]; check against TLC monthly vehicles_per_day and avg_hours_per_day_per_vehicle]; 0 to ~1,500 per zone.
impact_evidence: Matching collapses into long pickups when idle supply thins (Castillo, Knoepfle & Weyl 2017) [P, re-read by fact-check]; 243M app trips in 2025 (TLC budget testimony, Mar 2026) [S] [corrected by fact-check: a count of the 2025 HVFHV records gives 243,589,684 trips, about 667k/day; S, FerrisSearch analysis on GitHub]; online totals are [design] arithmetic.
data_source: TLC monthly report CSV (vehicles_per_day, avg_hours_per_day_per_vehicle, unique_drivers) https://www.nyc.gov/assets/tlc/downloads/csv/data_reports_monthly.csv ; HVFHV trip records https://www.nyc.gov/site/tlc/about/tlc-trip-record-data.page
how_to_model: Supply field per zone x 15 min, scaled so citywide vehicle-hours match the TLC monthly report and local pickup times match HVFHV request-to-on-scene times [corrected by fact-check: Uber rows only; Lyft (HV0005) leaves on_scene_datetime empty on ~99.7% of trips, S, fleetsim notes on GitHub].

name: Idle cars per open request (local balance)
description: Ratio of idle competing cars to unserved requests in a zone at a moment; it sets how fast any one driver gets a ping and whether surge fires.
values_or_range: 0.2 (shortage: surge, long pickups) to >10 (glut: long idle); about 1/3 of taxi and app cars in the Manhattan core are empty at any moment (2013-2017 data).
impact_evidence: Schaller, Empty Seats, Full Streets (2017): about one-third of vehicles in the Manhattan CBD empty [S]; thin idle supply triggers wild goose chases [P, re-read by fact-check].
how_to_model: Computed each tick from idle background cars and pending requests per zone; feeds ping rate, the surge model (R07) and pickup ETAs.

name: Trip market shares by service
description: Share of trips served by Uber, Lyft, yellow taxis, green taxis and other bases, which sets how many requests flow through each channel the agent can use.
values_or_range: 2025: app (HVFHV) about 667k trips/day (243.6M), Uber ~72% (176.0M) and Lyft ~28% (67.6M) [corrected by fact-check: full-year counts of the 2025 HVFHV records, S, FerrisSearch analysis on GitHub] (Lyft 27.7% in Sep 2025); yellow about 130k/day (+16% 2024 to 2025, 57% of the 2019 level); green ~1-2k/day [U]; other bases (black car, livery, luxury) are small [corrected by fact-check: the ~1,059 'other' entries are a cumulative base-number list kept in a GitHub repo, not a count of bases active in 2025].
impact_evidence: TLC testimony 17 Mar 2026 (243M app trips; taxi trips +16%, 57% of 2019) [S]; Uber/Lyft split from third-party analysis of TLC data [S]; a base map lists 30 Uber, 2 Lyft, 2 Via, 4 Juno and 1,059 other base numbers [S, re-read on GitHub by fact-check]; licence codes HV0002 Juno, HV0003 Uber, HV0004 Via, HV0005 Lyft [S, re-read].
data_source: TLC trip records (hvfhs_license_num: HV0003 Uber, HV0005 Lyft); FHV Base Aggregate Report https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Transportation/FHV-Base-Aggregate-Report/2v9c-2k7f ; https://github.com/toddwschneider/nyc-taxi-data
how_to_model: Split generated requests into channels by zone-hour shares from trip records; each channel has its own matcher and background fleet.

name: Active yellow taxi fleet
description: How many of the 13,587 medallions are actually on the road, competing for street hails and taxi e-hails.
values_or_range: About 10,520 active and about 3,069 in storage (Sep 2025) [uncertain: these sum to 13,589, not 13,587; source not re-checked]; over 1,000 medallions back on the road since Sep 2024; about 3-5k on the road in a daytime hour [corrected by fact-check: was 5-8k [U], which ~130k trips/day cannot keep busy; design calc as in R06-001].
impact_evidence: AutoMarketplace analysis of TLC data, Sep 2025 [S]; 13,587 medallion total [U].
how_to_model: Scale the yellow bot fleet to the scenario date; each taxi bot has a shift schedule and a cruising policy.

name: Green taxi fleet and hail zone
description: Size of the green (boro taxi) fleet, which may street-hail only outside Manhattan south of E 96th / W 110th St and outside the airports.
values_or_range: Small: ~1-2k trips/day and a few hundred to ~1,000 active cars [U]; the hail-exclusion zone is fixed: Manhattan south of E 96th St and W 110th St plus the NYC airports; green cars also may not start pre-arranged (base or app) trips in that Manhattan zone, though they may at airports [P*, 35 RCNY 51-03 and 82-13, verified by fact-check].
impact_evidence: Green volume shrank as app trips grew; no 2025-26 vehicle count found [U].
data_source: TLC green trip records; TLC monthly report (Green rows)
how_to_model: Small bot fleet restricted to outer-borough and upper-Manhattan hail polygons; matters only if the agent plays a green taxi.

name: Licensed pool versus active supply
description: Headroom between licensed cars and drivers and those actually working, which limits how many extra cars can flood in for surge or events.
values_or_range: 82,225 licensed app (HVFHV) vehicles; 179,670 licensed taxi and FHV drivers (TLC 2025); a fraction works on any one day (~40-60% [U]).
impact_evidence: TLC annual report 2025 [S]; daily share from TLC monthly vehicles_per_day vs unique_vehicles [U values].
data_source: TLC annual report https://www.nyc.gov/assets/tlc/downloads/pdf/annual_report_2025.pdf ; TLC monthly report
how_to_model: Cap on total background drivers who can log on; the entry model draws from the inactive pool.

name: Competitor product and vehicle-class mix
description: Share of competing cars eligible for each product (standard, XL, Comfort, Black/Lux, wheelchair-accessible, Green/EV), since dispatch only matches within eligible classes.
values_or_range: Mostly standard; XL ~10-15%, Black/Lux ~5% [U]; wheelchair-accessible cars served about 9% of 2025 app trips (21.4M of 243.6M had wav_match_flag = Y) [corrected by fact-check: was ~5-10% of cars [U]; S, FerrisSearch analysis on GitHub]; EV share rising (Green Rides target for 2030).
impact_evidence: Public app trip data has no product field, only wheelchair request/match flags [S, schema read on GitHub]; class shares [U].
data_source: None found for the XL/Comfort/Black mix; HVFHV wav_match_flag gives the WAV share of trips [S]; NYC Open Data active FHV vehicle list (make, model, WAV) [U]
how_to_model: Give each bot a vehicle class and keep separate supply pools per product; the agent's own class (R08) decides which pool it competes in.

name: Informal and unlicensed competition
description: Dollar vans, unlicensed livery cars and illegal street pickups by app cars, which take cheap short trips and hails in some neighbourhoods and at let-outs. Informal transit exists in other cities too, but its size is local.
values_or_range: TLC chair (Oct 2024): 35 TLC-licensed commuter vans vs 215 in 2019. Other counts: 31 in service (THE CITY); 38 licensed vehicles at 12 bases (City Council, 2024); 584 licensed in 2015. A state insurance-subsidy programme from Sep 2024 was credited with a 50% rise in licensed vans. Many more unlicensed vans run on the Flatbush Ave, Jamaica and Chinatown corridors [U]. Ridership is about 120,000/day (King & Goldwyn 2014 estimate; about 125,000 in a recent Economist piece) [S, dated]. Demand lost: 0-10% of short trips in affected zones [design].
impact_evidence: [S] City Limits and Next City (TLC chair, Oct 2024); amNY (City Council 2024 counts); ridership via an ASU study citing King & Goldwyn 2014. No current official ridership count exists. [corrected: ridership '~100k+ [U]' replaced by dated estimates].
data_source: TLC commuter-van licensing (counts via press); none found for unlicensed activity
how_to_model: Remove a zone-hour share of short-trip and hail demand before generation. Illegal hail competitors at let-outs reduce taxi hail encounters (R05-042).

name: Shift start (log-on) times
description: When competing drivers start work, by hour and weekday, mixing full-time and part-time drivers.
values_or_range: Weekday start peaks around 5-8 am and 3-6 pm [U]; full-time drivers gave ~80% of app rides (2018); 60-65% of yellow drivers are full-time (2026).
impact_evidence: Parrott & Reich 2018 report for TLC [S]; TLC testimony 17 Mar 2026 [S].
data_source: TLC monthly report (avg_hours_per_day_per_driver, avg_days_drivers_on_road); 2010-2013 yellow trips with hashed driver IDs https://databank.illinois.edu/datasets/IDB-9610843 [U]
how_to_model: Draw each bot's start time from an hour x weekday distribution fitted to supply curves; full-time (10-12 h) and part-time (2-5 h) types.

name: Shift end (log-off) rule
description: What makes competitors stop: hours worked, a daily income target, fatigue, or a legal cap on hours.
values_or_range: Stop after 8-12 h, or at an income target of $200-350/day [design]; TLC fatigue rule: at most 10 h of passenger time in any 24 h (the count resets after 8 consecutive hours with no passengers) and 60 h per Monday-Sunday week; time between trips does not count [corrected by fact-check: P*, 35 RCNY 80-14(f)].
impact_evidence: Camerer et al. 1997 found negative wage elasticity (income targeting) among NYC cab drivers; Uber data shows supply rising with surge (Chen & Sheldon) [S]; later NYC cab work (Farber 2015, QJE) finds little income targeting, so the evidence is mixed [U, added by fact-check].
data_source: 2010-2013 yellow trips with driver IDs (Illinois Data Bank) [U]
how_to_model: Log-off hazard = f(hours online, earnings vs target, time of day), fitted to shift-length distributions.

name: Short-run surge entry
description: How strongly offline drivers log on, or online drivers stay longer, when surge or earnings rise.
values_or_range: Supply elasticity to hourly earnings of 0.2-1.0 within 15-60 min; lag 5-30 min [design].
impact_evidence: Chen & Sheldon (Uber, US cities 2014-15): surge raises driver supply when surge is high [S].
data_source: None public for NYC; calibrate to how fast HVFHV pickup times recover after demand spikes
how_to_model: Entry rate = base x (1 + e x (surge - 1)) with a lag; lower log-off hazard during surge.

name: Surge chasing
description: Share of idle competitors who drive toward surge or busy zones, and how fast, which wears surge away before late arrivals get there.
values_or_range: 10-40% of idle drivers within 2-3 km respond; reaction lag 2-10 min [design]; surge recomputed every ~1-5 min [U].
impact_evidence: Driver interviews report surge often gone on arrival (Lee et al. 2015, CHI) [U]; ranges [design].
how_to_model: Bot policy: with probability p move toward the zone with the best expected earnings within a radius; produces herding.

name: Long-run re-equilibration
description: After fares or earnings stay higher for weeks, drivers add hours until utilisation falls and hourly pay returns near its old level.
values_or_range: Hourly earnings back near baseline about 2 months after an Uber fare rise.
impact_evidence: Hall, Horton & Knoepfle, NBER w30883, Ride-Sharing Markets Re-Equilibrate (2023) [S].
how_to_model: For multi-day and learning runs (10 days then day 11), drift background supply day by day so competitor hourly pay tends to a target; off in single-day runs.

name: Home anchoring of competitors
description: Competitors start and end shifts near home (mostly Queens, Brooklyn, the Bronx, NJ, Long Island), so supply is rich in the outer boroughs early and drains from Manhattan late.
values_or_range: Home mix e.g. Queens 35-45%, Brooklyn 20-25%, Bronx 15-20%, other 15-25% [U]; 10-20% of late-evening idle cars heading home [design].
impact_evidence: NYC app drivers are mostly immigrants living in the outer boroughs (Parrott & Reich 2018) [U]; mix [U].
data_source: None public for app drivers' homes; first and last pickups per shift in 2010-2013 taxi data [U]; Census ACS commute data [U]
how_to_model: Each bot has a home zone; shifts start there and the last hour is biased toward home (uses the destination filter).

name: Competitor breaks
description: Short supply dips when many drivers pause at once for meals, prayer, bathrooms or rest.
values_or_range: Lunch 12-2 pm; dinner or iftar at sunset; Friday midday prayers; 10-45 min break per 4-6 h [U].
impact_evidence: [design guess]; an evening dip in Ramadan was reported by Uber in Paris (2017) [S].
how_to_model: Break hazard by time of day per bot type; break spots near food and parking clusters (R01).

name: Competitor multi-apping share
description: Share of competitors logged into Uber and Lyft at once, so one car counts as supply on both and vanishes from both when matched.
values_or_range: US, Q1 2024: ~55% of Lyft drivers also on Uber, ~25% of Uber drivers also on Lyft; NYC share unknown.
impact_evidence: Gridwise driver-panel data [S]; Chicago's TNP driver data flags drivers reported by more than one company (MULTIPLE_TNPS) [S]; NYC's cruising rule already splits a car's idle time across platforms when it is available to more than one HVFHS [P*, 35 RCNY 59D-21(b)(1), added by fact-check].
how_to_model: Flag bots single- or dual-app; dual-app bots sit in both platforms' idle pools and take the better offer.

name: Competitor acceptance and cherry-picking
description: How often competitors decline offers (short, low pay, long pickup, unwanted destination), pushing those offers down the line to the agent.
values_or_range: Acceptance 50-95% by driver type [U]; top Uber Pro tiers need 90%+ acceptance in some markets.
impact_evidence: Uber Pro terms (Hong Kong) require 90%+ acceptance for top tiers [S]; NYC values [U]; NYC lets platforms restrict a driver's access without the usual 72 h notice for excessive cancellation or non-acceptance [P*, 35 RCNY 59D-22(c)(3), added by fact-check].
how_to_model: Bot accept probability = logistic(pay per minute, pickup ETA, destination); declined offers go back to the matcher.

name: Competitor strategy mix
description: Mix of background driver policies (cruiser, hotspot parker, airport queuer, surge chaser, home-anchored commuter, cherry-picker), with skill differences.
values_or_range: e.g. 30% hotspot parkers, 20% cruisers, 15% airport queuers, 15% surge chasers, 10% commuters, 10% random [design]; earnings-per-hour spread of +/-20-30% [U].
impact_evidence: Experience and where/when choices explain earnings gaps among Uber drivers (Cook et al. 2021) [U]; mix [design].
how_to_model: Bot population with archetype policies; mix tuned so zone supply and airport queue lengths match data.

name: Taxi 4-5 pm shift change
description: Yellow taxis go off duty to hand over at garages (mostly in Queens) in the late afternoon, cutting taxi supply just as demand rises.
values_or_range: Taxis on the road fell from 6,688 to 5,452 between 4 and 5 pm (2011), an 18.5% drop vs the hour before [corrected by fact-check: arithmetic; was 'about 20%'].
impact_evidence: TLC 2011 study via DNAinfo; later city GPS review [S].
how_to_model: Two-shift lease bots hand over at 4-5 pm with a deadhead to garage zones; check today's dip in 2024-26 yellow pickups by hour.

name: Cruising versus parking when idle
description: Whether idle competitors cruise (taxis hunting hails) or park and wait for pings (app drivers), which changes hail odds and congestion.
values_or_range: Empty time between passengers in the Manhattan core: 8 min for yellow vs 11 min for app cars (2017); app cars empty 41% of the time south of 96th St (2019).
impact_evidence: Schaller 2017 [S]; TLC data cited in the 2019 cruising-cap ruling [S].
how_to_model: Taxi bots cruise high-hail routes; app bots park near hotspots or drift; both feed the traffic model (R10).

name: Competitor information level as its own setting
description: How much public event, weather and calendar information the background bots act on (share of informed bots and their lead time), set separately from the agent's information arm.
values_or_range: Share of informed bots 0 / 25 / 50 / 100%; lead time 0-120 min; crossed with the agent's arm (R03-060, R04-049) in a 2x2 or 3x2 design [design].
impact_evidence: [P, from list] R06-052 ties bot event knowledge to the agent's treatment arm, which mixes two effects into one; [design].
how_to_model: The bot policy reads the same info feeds through a per-bot access flag. The experiment matrix crosses bot and agent information levels.

name: Incumbent platform response to the fleet
description: How Uber, Lyft and their drivers react when a fleet takes share, with targeted rider discounts, driver incentives or price cuts in the fleet's zones.
values_or_range: Competitor price cut of 0-5% per 10 points of share the fleet takes [design]. In San Francisco, Waymo's premium over Uber narrowed from about 31% (Mar-Apr 2025) to about 12.7% (Thanksgiving to New Year 2025, ~100k rides), cause unknown (R07-061) [S].
impact_evidence: [S] Obi price studies via TechCrunch (Jun 2025), Singularity Hub (Feb 2026) and Business Insider; primary Obi report not read. Holding competitor prices fixed overstates what a new entrant can win; R06-012 and R06-068 cover driver supply, not platform pricing.
how_to_model: A competitor price multiplier in the fleet's zones responds, with a lag of days, to the fleet's recent share; off in single-car mode.

name: Matching algorithm
description: How the platform pairs requests and drivers: send the nearest idle driver at once, or optimise over a short batch.
values_or_range: First-dispatch nearest | batched matching every 2-10 s (Uber: a few seconds) | global minimum total ETA.
impact_evidence: Uber's marketplace page describes batched matching over a few seconds [S]; first-dispatch causes wild goose chases when prices are low (Castillo et al.) [P, re-read by fact-check].
how_to_model: Pluggable matcher; default batched assignment over idle drivers within the radius every 5 s; sensitivity-test the window.

name: Matching cost metric
description: What 'closest' means: straight-line distance, road travel time, or travel time with penalties for wrong heading, U-turns and bridges.
values_or_range: Straight-line | road ETA (R10) | road ETA + heading penalty.
impact_evidence: [design]; Uber says batching lowers average wait [S]; a Manhattan HVFHV replay found batched min-cost assignment cut rider wait 5.3% and pickup deadhead 8.2% vs greedy nearest-car dispatch (fleetsim, GitHub) [S, added by fact-check].
data_source: OpenStreetMap road graph; NYC DOT speeds (R10)
how_to_model: Use road ETA from the traffic model; penalise drivers pointed the wrong way on one-way avenues.

name: Maximum dispatch radius
description: Furthest a driver can be sent for a pickup; beyond it the request waits or fails.
values_or_range: 8-15 min pickup cap typical [U]; a small radius avoids wild goose chases but leaves riders queued.
impact_evidence: Castillo et al.: a small maximum dispatch radius avoids wild goose chases but creates passenger queues [P, re-read by fact-check].
data_source: None (platform internal); infer from the tail of HVFHV request-to-on-scene times
how_to_model: Parameter r_max in minutes; unmatched requests retry each batch, then cancel by rider patience (R05).

name: Forward dispatch
description: The platform offers the next trip to a driver who is about to drop off, competing with nearby idle drivers.
values_or_range: On/off; look-ahead 0-5 min before drop-off [U].
impact_evidence: [U] Uber and Lyft send next-trip offers before drop-off.
how_to_model: Busy drivers with <= L minutes left join the matching pool; cost = time left + ETA from the drop-off.

name: Offer timeout and decline cascade
description: How long a driver has to accept, and how a declined or expired offer moves to the next driver.
values_or_range: About 10 s traditionally, 15 s in an Uber pilot [uncertain: not re-checked; driver guides often give ~15 s as Uber's standing window]; cascade to the next-best driver 3-5 times [U].
impact_evidence: The Rideshare Guy on Uber extending ping time [S].
how_to_model: Offer queue per request; simulated time pauses for the agent's decision (latency handled as a harness setting, R12).

name: Broadcast offers (Trip Radar)
description: Some requests are shown to several drivers at once and go to the first to accept, which rewards speed.
values_or_range: 0-20% of requests broadcast [design]; first to accept wins.
impact_evidence: Uber Trip Radar blog and driver reports of first-come matching [S].
how_to_model: Broadcast unmatched requests to k drivers; winner is first accept in simulated time, so LLM wall-clock latency does not count.

name: Product eligibility and opt-ins
description: Which request types a car can receive (X, XL, Comfort, Black, Green/EV, wheelchair), including higher classes opting into lower ones.
values_or_range: Yes/no per product; Black and XL drivers can opt into X [U].
impact_evidence: Uber-Waymo: robotaxis matched to UberX, Green, Comfort and Comfort Electric requests [S]; opt-in rules [U].
how_to_model: Each request carries a product; the matcher filters eligible cars; the agent can toggle opt-ins.

name: Wheelchair and Access-A-Ride dispatch
description: Wheelchair-accessible requests and paratransit trips go only to accessible cars, under service-level targets.
values_or_range: Flags wav_request_flag, wav_match_flag and access_a_ride_flag in the app trip data; WAV-requested and WAV-matched trips about 699k of 243.6M in 2025 (~0.3%) [corrected by fact-check: column names re-read on GitHub; share from FerrisSearch analysis [S]]; accessible taxis must accept dispatches from the Accessible Taxi Dispatcher [P*, 35 RCNY 53-08].
impact_evidence: HVFHV columns [S, read on GitHub]; accessible licences are the only new FHV licences in 2026 [S].
how_to_model: Separate accessible request stream; accessible cars get priority dispatch.

name: Shared-ride matching
description: Pooling riders into one car adds detours and changes per-trip pay.
values_or_range: shared_request_flag and shared_match_flag in the data; 2025: about 6.8M shared requests (2.8% of app trips, all Uber), of which 3.9M matched (1.6%) [corrected by fact-check: was 'small share [U]'; S, FerrisSearch analysis on GitHub].
impact_evidence: HVFHV columns [S]; pooling makes wild goose chases worse (Castillo et al.) [P].
how_to_model: Optional insertion heuristic; off in v1.

name: Taxi e-hail channel
description: Taxis also get app dispatches through Uber, Curb or Arro, a second request stream.
values_or_range: 5-25% of yellow trips via e-hail [U]; rising since Uber and Curb began dispatching cabs.
impact_evidence: AutoMarketplace: yellow trips +17-20% year on year (Aug-Sep 2025), driven by returning cabs and Uber/Curb e-hail [S].
data_source: Partial: yellow and green payment_type = 0 marks Flex Fare (upfront-priced e-hail) trips, a lower bound on e-hail [corrected by fact-check: was 'none found'; P* via R07 dictionary excerpt]; metered e-hail trips are not flagged
how_to_model: Route a share of app requests to taxis through a taxi e-hail matcher.

name: Wild goose chase threshold
description: Point where idle supply is so thin that matches go to far-away drivers, pickups lengthen, cancellations spike and pay falls.
values_or_range: Appears when idle density falls below the level where pickup ETA climbs steeply (city-specific) [design].
impact_evidence: Castillo, Knoepfle & Weyl: in thin hours and areas of Manhattan many riders and drivers cancel and waits jump [P, re-read by fact-check].
how_to_model: Emerges from matcher, r_max and rider patience; include a capped-surge scenario to test it.

name: Equal dispatch treatment of agent and background cars
description: Whether the simulated matcher, offer timeout, dispatch radius, tier perks and penalties treat the agent's cars exactly like the background bots.
values_or_range: Parity (default) / documented deviations. Checks: the agent's share of offers vs bots at equal ETA, decline-cascade timing, and tier perks (R09-041) applied by state, not by identity [design].
impact_evidence: [design]. [S, from list] Real apps have priority tiers (Uber Pro, R09-041), so any perk must be applied the same way to both.
how_to_model: The matcher sees only vehicle state, not identity. A parity test runs a scripted clone of a bot as the 'agent' and checks that its offer rates match the bots'.

name: Airport queue length and position
description: First-in-first-out virtual queue in airport waiting lots; the app shows your position and how many drivers are ahead.
values_or_range: 0 to 500+ cars; position visible; JFK Cell Phone Lot and Limo Lot.
impact_evidence: Uber JFK driver page [S]; Gridwise crowdsourced queue counts [S].
data_source: Uber JFK page; HVFHV pickups in airport zones
how_to_model: One FIFO per airport and platform; inflow from drop-offs and arrivals, outflow = airport requests.

name: Airport queue rules
description: Rules for keeping your place: stay inside the zone, stay online, do not decline or cancel repeatedly; lot capacity.
values_or_range: Lose place if offline, outside the zone, several declines or cancels in a row; a rider cancel does not cost the place.
impact_evidence: Uber JFK driver page [S].
how_to_model: Geofence plus queue state machine; overflow turned away when the lot is full [design].

name: Taxi hold lot and short-return ticket
description: Yellow taxis queue in JFK and LGA holding lots; a short trip to nearby areas earns a ticket to an expedited line if they return in time.
values_or_range: 2-hour return window (since 2012); JFK short-return area = Queens, Brooklyn, Five Towns [uncertain: window length and area not re-checked; the notice is on nyc.gov, which was blocked].
impact_evidence: TLC industry notice 12-33 [S].
how_to_model: Ticket state with expiry; priority lane in the taxi queue.

name: Airport rematch and priority tiers
description: A driver dropping off at the airport may get a pickup before joining the queue; top-tier drivers get priority.
values_or_range: Uber Pro Diamond/Platinum priority rematch (Australia, Hong Kong); NYC unknown.
impact_evidence: Uber Australia blog; Uber Hong Kong Pro terms [S].
how_to_model: At drop-off, probability p of a rematch from the queue head, higher for top tiers.

name: Airport queue service rate
description: How fast airport queues drain, set by arriving passengers' ride requests on each platform.
values_or_range: Depends on flight arrivals; 2025 app pickups: LGA 4.92M (~13.5k/day) and JFK 4.07M (~11.2k/day), ~25k/day combined, and the two top app pickup zones by revenue [corrected by fact-check: was ~10-25k/day [U]; S, FerrisSearch analysis of 2025 HVFHV records].
impact_evidence: [S] 2025 HVFHV counts; flight data is a cross-link to R03 and R05.
data_source: HVFHV pickups in airport zones; BTS on-time data https://www.transtats.bts.gov ; Port Authority traffic reports
how_to_model: Airport request process tied to the arrivals schedule, split by platform share.

name: Product-specific airport queues
description: App airport queues are kept per product tier, so an XL, Black or WAV car can wait in a much shorter line than an X car at the same airport. Extends R06-040 and R06-042 (one queue per airport and platform). Lot rules are airport-specific; generalise with a per-airport rule table.
values_or_range: A separate virtual queue per airport x platform x product (X/Comfort, XL, Black/SUV, WAV). At LGA, UberX and XL wait in the FHV Hold Lot (46-10 Berrian Blvd). Black and Black SUV wait in the Cell Phone Lot on 94th St between Astoria Blvd and 23rd Ave. Both lots are open 06:00-01:00. Where a car parks inside the lot does not change its place. Per-product queue lengths: none found (design default: XL queue 0.2-0.5x and Black 0.1-0.3x the X queue). WAV queue handling: none found.
impact_evidence: [S] Uber LaGuardia driver page via search snippets (uber.com unreachable from here): separate lots for X/XL and Black/Black SUV, open 6 am-1 am; a driver loses their place if offline, outside the zone or after repeated cancels. [uncertain: 2020-21 guides describe different lot layouts, so check the current page]. [U] The app shows queue position per product. Queue sizes are [design].
applies_to: human app driver (XL/Black/WAV vs X); fleet vehicle-class mix; robotaxi only if airports are in the ODD
data_source: Uber airport driver pages https://www.uber.com/drive/new-york/airports/laguardia-airport/ ; HVFHV airport-zone pickups (zones 132 JFK, 138 LGA; product not recorded); none found for per-product queue lengths
how_to_model: One FIFO queue per airport x platform x product. Service rate = airport requests for that product (product mix from R05-024). A car joins every queue it is eligible for, including opt-ins (R06-029); its first offer removes it from all of them.

sub_box: Robotaxis, rival model fleets and incumbent response
name: Robotaxi background fleet
description: Number of driverless cars competing in the scenario city.
values_or_range: NYC 2026: none carrying passengers (test permit Aug 2025 for 8 cars with safety drivers, expired 31 Mar 2026; state law allows testing only); scenarios 0-10% of supply; Waymo US ~3,000 cars in early 2026 [S] [uncertain: the 3,800 upper figure from the May 2026 recall was not re-checked].
impact_evidence: TechCrunch; West Side Spirit; fleet count from a May 2026 NHTSA recall [S]; NYC facts (Aug 2025 approval, 8 cars, specialist behind the wheel, Manhattan south of 112th St and Downtown Brooklyn, permits expired 31 Mar 2026, Hochul's Feb 2026 proposal withdrawn, ~3,000 US cars) match Vital City's Waymo map methodology on GitHub [S, re-checked by fact-check].
how_to_model: Scenario parameter; robotaxi bots never log off and charge at depots.

sub_box: Robotaxis, rival model fleets and incumbent response
name: Robotaxis on a human platform
description: When a platform mixes robotaxis and human drivers, which riders get which, and at what price.
values_or_range: Uber-Waymo in Austin and Atlanta: UberX, Green, Comfort and Comfort Electric requests can go to a Waymo at the same price, with no tip prompt; ~100 robotaxis in Austin (2025) and ~200 by 2026 [corrected by fact-check: these are analyst estimates, not Waymo disclosures, per Vital City's methodology on GitHub [S]].
impact_evidence: Uber investor release (2024); Reuters via StreetInsider [S].
how_to_model: Matcher includes robotaxis for eligible products inside the geofence, with a preference weight and a rider opt-out rate [U].

sub_box: Robotaxis, rival model fleets and incumbent response
name: Number of competing model fleets
description: How many LLM agents, each running 1 or N cars, compete in the same market.
values_or_range: 1 (solo against bots) up to 5 models x N cars.
impact_evidence: Multi-agent rankings differ from solo ones in Vending-Bench Arena (team dossier D07) [S].
how_to_model: Harness setting with seat rotation and mirrored runs (R12).

sub_box: Robotaxis, rival model fleets and incumbent response
name: Coordination channel between rival fleets
description: Whether competing agents can message each other, with a risk of zone-splitting collusion.
values_or_range: None | public | private.
impact_evidence: LLM agents formed cartels when given email in Vending-Bench Arena (team dossier D07) [S].
how_to_model: Harness toggle; log messages and detect zone partitioning.

sub_box: Robotaxis, rival model fleets and incumbent response
name: Tacit collusion between model fleets
description: In a shared city, model fleets that set prices or supply can drift to matching high prices or withheld supply (or into price wars) without ever messaging each other. Explicit messaging is R06-065.
values_or_range: Metrics: a price index between a competitive (Nash) benchmark and the monopoly price; supply withdrawal in contested zones. Rule: allowed but reported / penalised above a threshold [design].
impact_evidence: [S] Fish, Gonczarowski & Shorrer, 'Algorithmic Collusion by Large Language Models' (arXiv 2404.00806, v5 5 Mar 2026): LLM pricing agents quickly and autonomously reach supracompetitive prices, and prompt wording changes how far. [S] Calvano, Calzolari, Denicolo & Pastorello (AER 110(10), 2020): Q-learning pricing agents collude without communicating. [P*, from list] Vending-Bench Arena cartels (R12-049).
how_to_model: An arena-mode monitor computes price and supply indices per zone-hour, anchored by competitive and monopoly reference policies, and reports a collusion index beside the scores.

name: Background supply generation mode
description: How the simulator creates competitor cars: replay historical trips as ghost drivers, simulate rule-based bots, or a hybrid.
values_or_range: Replay | agent-based bots | hybrid (replayed demand, bot supply).
impact_evidence: [design]; public app trip data has no driver or vehicle ID, so driver-level replay is impossible [S, columns re-read on GitHub by fact-check]; the TLC may collect driver and vehicle licence numbers per trip (Admin Code 19-550(d)) but does not publish them [P*].
how_to_model: Default hybrid: demand resampled from trips; supply from a calibrated bot population.

name: Displacement rule for replayed trips
description: When the agent serves a request that a background driver served in history, what happens to that driver.
values_or_range: Remove the trip from the background driver (it idles) | ignore (additive) | full re-simulation.
impact_evidence: [design].
how_to_model: Background bots re-plan after losing a trip, so each request is served once.

name: Supply elasticity setting
description: Whether background supply is fixed or reacts to surge, events, agent behaviour and earnings.
values_or_range: Fixed | short-run elastic | short- and long-run elastic.
impact_evidence: Chen & Sheldon; Hall et al. [S].
how_to_model: Toggle; report scores under both to separate skill from equilibrium effects.

name: Double-counting guard for replayed days
description: Weather, event, holiday and disruption modifiers apply only to a baseline with those effects removed, never on top of a replayed real day that already contains them.
values_or_range: Rule: a replayed day gets no modifiers, or only the difference between the scenario and what actually happened. A synthetic day gets a baseline cleaned of weather, events, holidays and outages, plus modifiers [design]. Reference days used to build baselines must be screened for data gaps (R02-065).
impact_evidence: [P] Own re-check on local yellow 2023 files. Replayed days already contain their shocks: on the 29 Sep 2023 flood day, yellow trips were +10% to +21% from 05:00-09:00 and -17% to -28% from 11:00-15:00 against 8 and 15 Sep and 6 and 13 Oct (day total -12%). [Corrected by fact-check: the +46-63% copied from R04-003 is very likely an artefact of using 22 Sep 2023 as a reference Friday. That day holds only 4,633 trips because of the TLC file gap (R02-065); with it in the reference set the morning shows +44-59%.] This is also a live example of a contaminated baseline. R03-066 removes only events from the baseline [design].
data_source: NYC TLC trip records; NOAA weather; event calendars (R03); MTA alerts
how_to_model: Fit a de-shocked baseline by regressing zone-hour demand on weather, event, holiday, outage and data-gap indicators, and add scenario modifiers only to that baseline. A unit test checks that a modifier is never applied on top of a replay that already contains it.

sub_box: Taxi meter, surcharges and flat fares
name: Airport fare and fee triggers
description: Fare rules switched on by airport geography (amounts owned by R07).
values_or_range: Taxi: JFK to/from Manhattan flat $70 (+$5 weekdays 4-8pm); LGA +$5 to and from; airport access fee on JFK/LGA taxi pickups $1.25 until Mar 2023 and $1.75 from Apr 2023 (trip records), possibly $2.00 in 2026 [uncertain: 2026 amount from a code comment only]. HVFHV: $2.50 airport fee on pickups and drop-offs at JFK/LGA/EWR, already in Jan 2023 records [corrected by fact-check: the original said 'since Apr 2023'; the April 2023 change was the taxi access fee rising to $1.75]. Newark taxi trips: meter + $20 surcharge + tolls both ways [corrected by fact-check: $20 is the rule in force, not a proposal]
impact_evidence: [P*] 35 RCNY 58-26(a)(2)(iii), (b), (c)(3); [P*] airport_fee values in yellow 2023-24 and HVFHV Jan 2023 records; [S] 2026 fare config quoting the TLC rate card; VisaVerge / Fox5 on the FHV fee
data_source: TLC fare page; airport_fee fields in trip records
how_to_model: Airport polygons trigger fare-engine branches

sub_box: Taxi meter, surcharges and flat fares
name: Taxi metered rate of fare
description: The yellow and green taxi meter charges an initial unit plus one unit per fifth of a mile when moving at 12 mph or more, or per 60 seconds when slower or stopped.
values_or_range: $3.00 initial + $0.70 per unit = $3.50/mile above 12 mph, $0.70/min (=$42/h) below 12 mph; unchanged since 18 Dec 2022 and still in force Aug 2026
impact_evidence: [P*] 35 RCNY 58-26(a) and 82-26(a), rules current through 13 Aug 2026 (re-read in fact-check)
data_source: 35 RCNY via nyc_code_archive (verbatim export, current to 13 Aug 2026) https://github.com/jehiah/nyc_code_archive; validate on yellow/green fare_amount in NYC TLC trip records https://www.nyc.gov/site/tlc/about/tlc-trip-record-data.page
how_to_model: Meter integrates the per-second speed trace from the travel-time engine: distance units above 12 mph, time units below (cross-link R10-043)

sub_box: Taxi meter, surcharges and flat fares
name: Final-unit pre-assessment (round-up)
description: The meter charges the full unit that is currently accruing, so every metered fare is rounded up to the next $0.70.
values_or_range: +$0.00 to +$0.70 per trip, about +$0.35 on average [design calc]
impact_evidence: [P*] 35 RCNY 58-26(a)(1)(i)-(v): initial unit $3.00, each additional unit $0.70, current unit pre-assessed
data_source: 35 RCNY via https://github.com/jehiah/nyc_code_archive; calibrate on yellow fare_amount vs trip_distance and duration
how_to_model: Fare = $3.00 + 0.70 x floor(accrued units) [corrected by fact-check: the $3.00 prices the initial unit (first 1/5 mi or 60 s) and $0.70 each additional unit, so the earlier $3.00 + 0.70 x ceil(units) charges one unit too many] [uncertain: which convention meters implement; calibrate on yellow fare_amount]

sub_box: Taxi meter, surcharges and flat fares
name: Weekday rush-hour surcharge
description: Flat surcharge on taxi trips that start in the weekday afternoon peak, except on legal holidays.
values_or_range: $2.50 for trips starting Mon-Fri after 16:00 and before 20:00, not on legal holidays; $5.00 on JFK-Manhattan flat-fare trips
impact_evidence: [P*] 35 RCNY 58-26(a)(2)(i) and (b)(1)(i); about 12% on a $20 meter fare [design calc]
data_source: 35 RCNY via https://github.com/jehiah/nyc_code_archive; yellow 'extra' field; holiday calendar from R02
how_to_model: Add by trip start timestamp and holiday flag; driver keeps it (part of fare)

sub_box: Taxi meter, surcharges and flat fares
name: Overnight surcharge
description: Flat surcharge on taxi trips that start at night.
values_or_range: $1.00 for trips starting after 20:00 and before 06:00 (not on JFK flat-fare trips [S])
impact_evidence: [P*] 35 RCNY 58-26(a)(2)(ii); [S] JFK flat-fare page lists no overnight charge (code comment citing TLC fare page)
how_to_model: Add by trip start time; driver keeps it

sub_box: Taxi meter, surcharges and flat fares
name: MTA State surcharge on taxi trips
description: State tax added to taxi trips that start in NYC and end in NYC or one of seven nearby counties; the driver collects it and the owner or e-hail app remits it.
values_or_range: $0.50 per trip; applies to destinations in NYC, Dutchess, Nassau, Orange, Putnam, Rockland, Suffolk, Westchester
impact_evidence: [P*] 35 RCNY 58-26(a)(3) and 80-17(g) list the counties; [P*] 35 RCNY 51-03 defines the MTA Tax as the 50-cent tax under NYS Tax Law Art. 29-A (amount upgraded from [S] by fact-check)
how_to_model: Add to rider total; exclude from driver revenue

sub_box: Taxi meter, surcharges and flat fares
name: Taxi improvement surcharge
description: Per-trip surcharge that the driver remits through the medallion (or green licence) owner to the City's Taxicab Improvement Fund, which pays for accessible taxis.
values_or_range: $1.00 per taxi trip and per green hail trip (levied since 1 Jan 2015; $0.30 before Dec 2022 [U])
impact_evidence: [P*] 35 RCNY 58-26(a)(1)(i) and (h), 80-17(h)-(i), 51-03 (deposited into the Taxicab Improvement Fund) [corrected by fact-check: fund money, not owner revenue]
how_to_model: Add to rider total; exclude from driver and owner revenue; optional WAV-taxi driver payments from the fund

sub_box: Taxi meter, surcharges and flat fares
name: Airport access fee on taxi pickups
description: Fee added to yellow taxi trips that pick up at JFK or LaGuardia, passed through to the airport operator.
values_or_range: $1.25 (older dictionary), then $1.75 in 2023-2025 records; one 2026 code source says the current TLC rate card shows $2.00 [S, unverified]; may change [uncertain: 2026 amount unresolved; rate card and 2026 trip files unreachable during fact-check]
impact_evidence: [P*] yellow dictionary (Mar 2025): 'For pick up only at LaGuardia and John F. Kennedy Airports'; [S] amounts from 2025 trip-data notebooks and a 2026 fare config
how_to_model: Add on pickups in zones 132 (JFK) and 138 (LGA); pass-through

sub_box: Taxi meter, surcharges and flat fares
name: LaGuardia surcharge
description: Flat surcharge on yellow taxi trips to and from LaGuardia (green taxis: trips to LaGuardia).
values_or_range: $5.00 per trip; recorded with fare extras and treated as driver revenue [U] (listed with rush and night surcharges in 58-26(a)(2); owners may not take surcharges above the lease, 58-21(c)(5))
impact_evidence: [P*] 35 RCNY 58-26(a)(2)(iii) and 82-26(a)(2)(iii); makes LGA runs about $5 more valuable than an equal metered trip
how_to_model: Add when origin or destination is zone 138 (yellow) or destination is 138 (green)

sub_box: Taxi meter, surcharges and flat fares
name: JFK-Manhattan flat fare
description: Fixed taxi fare between JFK and any Manhattan address in either direction; trips from JFK to other boroughs stay metered.
values_or_range: $70.00 + $5 weekday 16:00-20:00 + MTA tax, improvement, congestion, CBD and airport fees and tolls [uncertain: whether the airport access fee applies on RatecodeID 2 trips]; multi-stop: flat to first stop then meter
impact_evidence: [P*] 35 RCNY 58-26(b); [S] 2025 HVFHV: average base fare $73.18 for JFK pickups and $59.72 for LGA [corrected by fact-check: '$60-73' mixed the two], LGA/JFK the top revenue zones; driver bears the traffic risk on a fixed fare
data_source: 35 RCNY via https://github.com/jehiah/nyc_code_archive; RatecodeID = 2 in yellow records
how_to_model: If (JFK, Manhattan zone) pair, replace meter with $70; keep surcharges; time cost from R10-010

sub_box: Taxi meter, surcharges and flat fares
name: Newark Airport taxi trips
description: Taxi trips to Newark use the meter plus a surcharge, and the passenger pays tolls both ways; drivers may refuse EWR after 8 hours of operation in a 24-hour period.
values_or_range: Meter + $20.00 Newark surcharge + tolls out and back; NYC taxis may not solicit or cruise for fares at Newark Airport (80-19(a)(4)(i), upgraded from [U] by fact-check; prearranged EWR pickups not checked), so model an empty return
how_to_model: Add $20 and double tolls; force an empty return leg; allow refusal flag after 8 h

sub_box: Taxi meter, surcharges and flat fares
name: Out-of-city taxi fares
description: Rules for taxi trips leaving NYC: Westchester and Nassau use double meter beyond the city line; other places use a flat dollar fare agreed before departure.
values_or_range: Westchester/Nassau: in-city meter + 2x meter outside + tolls both ways; other counties: negotiated flat (RatecodeID 5); service to Westchester/Nassau is mandatory
impact_evidence: [P*] 35 RCNY 58-26(c), 80-17(f), 80-20(a)(1); rare trips but single fares of $100+ [U]
how_to_model: Split route at city boundary; double outside units; negotiated fare drawn from historical RatecodeID 5 distribution

sub_box: Taxi meter, surcharges and flat fares
name: Flex Fare (taxi e-hail upfront price)
description: TLC-approved e-hail apps can offer yellow and green taxi riders a binding upfront fare instead of the meter, using a filed rate schedule.
values_or_range: Optional per e-hail trip; recorded as payment_type 0; driver sees pickup, drop-off and quote before accepting; WAV requests may not cost more; apps include Curb, Arro and Uber's taxi integration [S]
impact_evidence: [P*] 35 RCNY 78-15(b), 78-21(a)(3), 80-17(a)(1), 51-03; [P*] yellow dictionary payment_type 0 = Flex Fare trip; shifts traffic risk to the driver
how_to_model: E-hail offers carry a fixed quote from an app pricing model (like R07-019); accepted Flex trips ignore the meter

sub_box: Taxi meter, surcharges and flat fares
name: Taxi revenue split by fare component
description: Which parts of a taxi fare the driver keeps and which pass to the owner, the state, the MTA, the City fund or the airport.
values_or_range: Driver keeps meter fare, rush/night/LGA extras and tips; MTA tax, congestion surcharge, CBD fee and airport fee are pass-through; improvement surcharge goes via the owner to the City's Taxicab Improvement Fund [corrected by fact-check]; owner may collect the MTA tax from the driver (58-21(c)(5)(vii)); tolls reimburse the E-ZPass holder
impact_evidence: [P*] 35 RCNY 80-17(g)-(i), 58-21(c)(5), 51-03; scoring on rider totals would overstate driver revenue by roughly $5-7 per Manhattan trip [design calc]
data_source: 35 RCNY via https://github.com/jehiah/nyc_code_archive; yellow/green itemised fare fields
how_to_model: Ledger with one row per fare component and a recipient (driver, owner, state, MTA, City fund, airport)

name: Hourly tipping
description: Share of trips tipped and tip size by hour.
values_or_range: HVFHV tip incidence 14-15% at 02-04h vs 22% at 11-12h, avg tip $0.67-1.17; yellow card tip/fare about 22% midday, 24-25% at 16-20h weekdays [corrected by fact-check: 14-15% holds for Sat/Sun 02-04h, weekday 02-04h is 15-18%; yellow 23.9-24.9% is 16-19h, 20h is 23.3%]
impact_evidence: [P*] own calc, TLC HVFHV Jan 2023; yellow 16-20h uplift likely because tip presets apply to totals incl. $2.50 surcharge [design inference]
how_to_model: Tip probability and size as functions of hour, payment type and fare

name: App tip propensity and amount
description: Whether an app rider tips and how much.
values_or_range: ~15-16% of UberX trips tipped (US, 2017 data); ~60% of riders never tip, 1% always [S]; [fact-check: NYC HVFHV Jan 2023: 19.6% of Uber and 18.8% of Lyft trips carry a tip, mean ~$5 when tipped; tips are 4.5-4.7% of base fare and 5.6-6.5% of driver pay, matching the '~4-5% of fare' secondary figure]; robotaxi tips none [U]
impact_evidence: [S] Chandar, Gneezy, List & Muir 2019 (NBER w26380); [P*] own calc on local TLC Parquet copies (HVFHV tips); [S] blog analysis of 243M HVFHS trips
how_to_model: Hurdle model: persistent rider tipper type x P(tip | context) x amount

name: Taxi tip (card defaults, cash unrecorded)
description: Taxi tips anchored by the card-screen tip buttons [uncertain: button sets differ by vendor and year (15/20/25% and 20/25/30% both reported) [U]]; cash tips are missing from the data.
